title: Distributed Lock with Fencing Tokens vs Redlock Split-Brain
subtitle: Preventing Stale Writes under Asynchronous Network Delays and Stop-The-World GC
problem_statement: A distributed file processing system uses Redis distributed locks (Redlock algorithm with 10-second TTL) to ensure only one worker modifies a shared S3 object at a time. Worker A acquires the lock, but encounters a 15-second full GC pause. The lock expires in Redis and is acquired by Worker B. Worker A wakes up and writes its stale buffer to S3, overwriting Worker B's fresh updates.

faded_bug.description: Mutating shared external storage using leased lock without monotonically increasing fencing token.

invariants.description: Zero stale writes allowed: storage must reject writes with smaller fencing tokens than last committed.

probing_ladder.stage_1_validation: Explain Martin Kleppmann's critique of the Redlock algorithm. Under what physical assumptions regarding clocks and network delays does Redlock fail?
probing_ladder.stage_2_tightening: What is a fencing token? How does the storage engine enforce that Client A's write with token 33 is rejected after Client B wrote with token 34?
probing_ladder.stage_3_adversarial: If the storage engine (e.g. standard file system) does NOT natively support atomic check-and-set or version precondition checks, how can you guarantee mutual exclusion?
probing_ladder.stage_4_squeeze: Why not use an active-active transactional consensus database (CockroachDB / Spanner) instead of maintaining distributed locks?

counter_probes.counter_question: Redlock relies on physical time elapsed across multiple Redis nodes. If one node's physical clock drifts forwards due to NTP jumps, can two clients hold the lock simultaneously?
counter_probes.expected_staff_answer: Yes. Redlock depends on physical time assumptions. Without monotonic fencing tokens validated by the resource server, no asynchronous lock algorithm can guarantee safety under GC pauses.
